kurz: Why the body reacts faster than the mind in a crash, why lows always come before the good news, and what must be settled beforehand.

bloecke.md:
A loss affects the body first and only then the mind. A portfolio that has lost 12% overnight is processed as a threat and not as a series of numbers. The amygdala reacts before any argument has been examined. Within seconds, pulse, blood pressure and muscle tone rise, and attention focuses entirely on the source of danger. Cortisol is released with a delay of a few minutes. The cortisol level remains elevated for hours, and in a stock market week with new lows every day practically permanently.

In 2008 the neuroscientist and former trader John Coates, together with Joe Herbert, found on a London trading floor that the traders' cortisol levels rose with market volatility. According to Coates's interpretation, persistently elevated cortisol makes people nervous and also systematically lowers their willingness to take risks. This happens precisely when risk has historically been best rewarded. A finding from brain scans by Kuhnen and Knutson (2005) fits this. There, risk-averse wrong decisions went hand in hand with activity in the anterior insula, a region that is also active during physical discomfort.

Panic is therefore not a character flaw. The stress response works correctly, but it reacts to a signal it did not evolve for.

In a crash, there is no lack of knowledge. The problem is the state in which it is called up. Severe stress narrows the time horizon to hours. A decision for twenty years is then made in a state in which you only think as far as the evening. Munger lists a tendency of its own for this. According to it, light stress sharpens judgement, while heavy stress destroys it.

## Two avoidance strategies

In addition, there is the familiar pattern of loss aversion, in an intensified form during a crash. Losses weigh around twice as heavily as gains of the same size. The meta-analysis by Brown and co-authors (2024) of 607 estimates arrives at a factor of about 1.96. Investors who look at their portfolio app every hour experience this factor dozens of times a day. Benartzi and Thaler (1995) described this as [[myopic loss aversion]]. Looking more often provides no additional information; it only produces the feeling of a loss more often.

This is followed by two reactions that contradict each other and yet both occur. One is [[action bias]], because acting feels better than doing nothing. The other is denial. It explains why many investors stop opening their portfolio at all during a crash. Both avoid the feeling of powerlessness, one through activity, the other through absence. In neither case is a decision made.

## Lows and the news

The intention “to wait until things calm down” fails because lows come before the good news, not after it.

The DAX reached its crisis low on 6 March 2009 at 3,666.41 points, around 55% below the high of 8,151.57 on 13 July 2007. On that day, the crisis following the Lehman bankruptcy was still in full swing. General Motors did not file for bankruptcy until three months later. German economic output shrank by around 5.7% in 2009. That was the sharpest slump of the post-war period, and it was only measured when prices had long been rising again.

In 2020 the pattern repeated itself in a shorter time. On 12 March 2020 the DAX lost 12.24% in a single day and closed at 9,161.13 points. That was the second-largest daily loss in its history. It reached its low on 18 March, four days before the start of the lockdown in Germany. The S&P 500 lost 33.9% in 33 calendar days and was back above its previous high on 18 August. That was almost three months before the first announcement of the efficacy of a coronavirus vaccine on 9 November. The DAX ended 2020 with a gain of 3.55%.

bloecke.titel: Two lows and the recovery that followed
bloecke.unter: In both crises, prices rose again before the news improved.

## Best and worst trading days

That is why the intention to get back in “when things calm down” is arithmetically expensive. Around 76% of the S&P 500's best trading days fell in a bear market or in the first two months of a new bull market. For the DAX, two of the three largest daily gains in its history fall in October 2008. An investor who had sold would still have been waiting for things to calm down during this phase.

bloecke.unter: Large swings up and down fall in the same weeks; 13 and 28 October 2008 were in the middle of the financial crisis.

bloecke.titel: A statistic told from one side
bloecke.md: The argument that “anyone who misses the ten best days loses half” is almost always presented one-sidedly. Bank of America calculated both sides for the S&P 500 from 1930 to March 2022. Fully invested, the cumulative return was 19,975%; without the ten best days in each decade, it was only 45%. Without the ten worst days in each decade, on the other hand, it would have been 4,275,143%. If both groups are missing, the result is 30,678%, only about 0.47 percentage points a year more than fully invested. The statement “timing costs you half” is therefore incomplete. The best and worst days lie in the same weeks and cannot be separated from each other.

## Depth and duration of declines

Nor can you say in advance how long a decline will last, and its depth does not tell you either. The coronavirus slump of 33.9% was recovered after 5.9 months. The less deep decline during the 2022 interest rate shock, at 25.4%, lasted 24.5 months, more than four times as long. The decline of 49.1% from 2000 lasted just over seven years.

bloecke.md:
## The cost of a panic sale

A sale during a crash is more than a pause. It immediately gives rise to a second decision, the one about getting back in. There is no point in time for this that feels good. Low prices seem dangerous, higher ones too expensive, and the old purchase price continues to act as an [[Anchoring effect|anchor]].

bloecke.titel: Illustrative calculation for an exit on 23 March 2020
bloecke.md:
The starting point is €100,000 at the high of 19 February 2020, invested in a broad equity ETF that tracks the S&P 500.

- Selling at the low (minus 33.9%) leaves €66,100, which is put into an instant-access savings account.
- On 18 August 2020 the index is back at the level of the previous high. If the units are only bought back at this point, the investment starts again with €66,100 instead of €100,000.
- The shortfall of 33.9% remains in percentage terms and grows in euros. At 7% a year, it takes around 6.1 years for the €66,100 alone to become €100,000 again. The portfolio without a sale keeps growing during this time.
- The calculation assumes a sale exactly at the low, that is, at the most unfavourable moment, and a buyback immediately at the previous high. Getting back in only after things have “calmed down” costs more.
In addition, there are tax consequences. A sale realises the price loss and also ends the tax deferral from which a long-held portfolio has benefited until then.

bloecke.titel: Tax consequences of a panic sale (Germany, as of 2026)
zeilen: Equity ETF, at a loss overall

Because of the 30% partial exemption (Teilfreistellung) for equity funds (Section 20 InvStG, Investment Tax Act), only 70% of the loss counts. This deductible part goes into the general loss pot and is offset against positive capital income of the same year and later years.

Because of the partial exemption (Section 20 InvStG), only 70% of the gain is taxable. On this, 25% flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) plus solidarity surcharge is due, 26.375% in total, plus church tax where applicable (Section 32d EStG, Income Tax Act). Without church tax, this amounts to around 18.46% of the entire gain. The benefit of many years of tax deferral is thus used up for good.
Goes into the share loss pot (Section 20(6) EStG) and can only be offset against gains from sales of shares in the same year and later years, not against interest, dividends or fund gains.
Fund units held in the crash year

If the calendar year ends with a loss in value, no advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale) is due, because it is capped at the increase in value during the calendar year (Section 18 InvStG). With accumulating funds, a loss year then costs no tax if you hold on.

bloecke.md:
## Kostolany's sleeping pill advice and its limits

The most popular piece of advice on the subject comes from André Kostolany. You should buy quality shares, take a sleeping pill and not look for years. Usually it is only half quoted. Kostolany explicitly applied it to the upward phase of his cycle, which he called A2. For the downward phase B2 he ruled out the sleeping pill. There he called for staying liquid and alert, because otherwise you miss the moment to get back in.

He determined the phases on the basis of trading volume and ownership, not the price. If prices fall on high volume, the shaky hands give up, and the securities pass to the strong hands. In this model, a crash is less a misfortune than a change of owners.

punkte: enough money not to have to sell anything
thoughts in the form of their own thesis, written down beforehand
patience for a phase that can last months or years
luck, and the knowledge that it is part of the game
little money, often borrowed or needed at short notice
no opinion of their own, plenty of other people's instead
no patience, checking the value every hour
no plan for the situation that is happening right now

bloecke.text: At the stock exchange, two times two is never four, but five minus one.

bloecke.md: Kostolany was an avowed speculator, worked with forward transactions and short sales and went bust twice. In 1931 he lost his entire fortune as a result of the Hoover Moratorium. His well-known anecdotes come from retold publishing material and have not been independently verified. As a role model for a private portfolio, he is only of limited use. Yet these bankruptcies are the source of his most important rule for a crash: never buy shares on credit. With a securities-backed loan, it is the broker who decides whether you hold out.

## Planning before the crash

In an acute state of stress, nothing helps that has to be decided in that very state. The only things that work are therefore those that were settled beforehand and require no further decision afterwards. This is the purpose of a crash protocol. It contains figures instead of motivational sentences, is written in advance and, when the crisis comes, is only read.

schritte.text: Work out what minus 30% and minus 50% would mean in euros for your own portfolio, with today's date. Percentages are underestimated in a crash, amounts are not.
Two or three sentences on why the portfolio is structured the way it is and which assumption would have to be wrong for anything about it to change. A falling price is not such an assumption.
The emergency fund and the money for all expenses in the next five years do not belong in the portfolio. This establishes in writing that there is no compulsion to sell in a crash.
Record the savings plan, contribution amount, execution day and rebalancing ranges. What runs without a decision cannot be decided wrongly in a state of stress.
Decide in advance what is permitted in a crash, for example a rebalancing order when the range is breached. Everything else needs a seven-day waiting period and a written justification.
Record the index level and portfolio value on the day of writing. After the crash, this sheet is the only reliable record, because your own memory smooths out the course of events in hindsight.

bloecke.md:
- Switch off the portfolio app's price push notifications and set a fixed, infrequent date for checking the portfolio.
- Keep the savings plan running, especially during a crash. It automatically buys more units without anyone having to decide.
- Check your exemption order (Freistellungsauftrag). The saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) is €1,000 per person and €2,000 for joint assessment (Section 20(9) EStG).
- Keep the emergency fund in a separate account, not in the settlement account of your securities account. Separate pots, otherwise often a cognitive bias, help here for once.

When the threshold is reached, a stop-loss order becomes a sell order without a price limit. If the market opens with a price gap far below it, the order is executed at the next tradable price and not at the threshold. In addition, there are volatility interruptions on Xetra and considerably widened bid-ask spreads for ETFs. Investors with tight stops sold in March 2020 immediately before the days that subsequently brought the recovery.

A crash protocol guarantees nothing. It makes decisions under stress harder and therefore less likely, but it does not prevent them. There are hardly any robust studies on how many investors stick to their written plan when it comes to the crunch.

Moreover, no plan protects against an investment becoming permanently worthless. With an individual company this happens; with a broadly diversified world index it has not happened historically. How broadly the portfolio is diversified therefore counts for more before the crash than any rule of behaviour during the crash.

mitnehmen: In a crash, decisions about an investment horizon of decades are made under stress that narrows the time horizon to hours; that is where the mistake lies, not in a lack of knowledge.
Lows systematically come before the good news; the S&P 500 was back at a record high on 18 August 2020, almost three months before the first vaccine announcement.
The best and the worst trading days lie in the same weeks; two of the DAX's three largest daily gains fell in October 2008.
The duration of a decline cannot be derived from its depth; the 2020 slump was deeper than that of 2022 and was recovered four times faster.
The only things that work are those that are set down in writing before the crash and require no further decision afterwards.

begriffe.text: Kostolany's term for investors who lack at least one of the first three of his four Gs: money (Geld), thoughts (Gedanken) or patience (Geduld). In a crash they sell to the strong hands, who have all four Gs: money, thoughts, patience and luck (Glück).
Phase at the end of a bear market in which, on high trading volume, even the last holders sell, although they find it hard to do so. It typically coincides with the worst news and the price low.
Brief trading halt on Xetra when the next price would leave a predefined range. It does not change the price, but makes orders without a price limit particularly risky in phases of panic.

Flat-rate tax-free portion of income from investment funds, 30% for equity funds held as private assets (Section 20 InvStG). It reduces the tax on gains and cuts the deductible loss to the same extent.

Document filled in beforehand with the portfolio value, loss amounts in euros, the reason for investing and permitted actions. In a crash it is only read, and looking things up takes the place of a decision.
